The life cycle of the black-lip pearl oyster begins with the release of fertilised eggs, each developing from an egg diameter of 67 micrometers, which yields an initial wet weight at birth of 0.00000016 grams [Wwb = 0.00000016 grams]. At a constant water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the embryonic period progresses rapidly, with the first larval stage, the trochophore, emerging from the egg after just 1 day [ab = 1 day]. This age at the birth stage is notably brief, though field observations frequently record a longer interval due to diapauses during incubation that can delay development. During the earliest phases of post-embryonic growth, the shell diameter remains minute, measuring merely 0.006 centimeters [Lb = 0.006 centimeters] at the prodissoconch I stage. This initial shell size is consistent with the small egg dimensions and represents the starting point for a dramatic increase in shell dimensions as the veliger larva begins exogenous feeding on phytoplankton.

Larval development proceeds through a series of well-defined morphological transitions, culminating in metamorphosis and settlement. At a water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the age at metamorphosis occurs at 18 days  following fertilisation, a duration that aligns with the relatively rapid development observed among tropical bivalves. At this critical juncture, the pediveliger larva attains a shell diameter of 0.0180 centimeters  before undergoing the metamorphic climax involving velum loss and gill development. The timing of this transition is temperature-sensitive, and the 28.1 °C thermal regime used in hatchery settings appears to accelerate progress relative to cooler conditions. Following settlement and the shift to benthic life, the newly metamorphosed juvenile, known as spat, begins the process of shell accretion that will characterise the remainder of its existence.

As juveniles mature into reproductively active adults, several key size thresholds define the species' growth trajectory. In populations that achieve a maximal shell height of 14 centimeters within a given family line, the shell height reaches 4 centimeters (4 cm) [Lp = 4 cm] during the transition to the sub-adult phase. This value represents an intermediate point in the growth curve, occurring well before the ultimate size is attained. The ultimate shell height of the species has been reported to range from 14 to 25 centimeters in various studies, but a maximal length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] is occasionally recorded in exceptionally favourable environments. This substantial maximal dimension distinguishes Pinctada margaritifera as one of the larger pearl oyster species, capable of producing high-quality nacre over a long growth period. The attainment of such size requires sustained access to nutrient-rich waters and stable hydrodynamic conditions.

At 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 50% [GSI = 50%]. This ratio was calculated from the surface area relationship between total flesh and gonad tissue. First reproduction occurs at 365 days after fertilisation [tR = 365 days after fertilisation] when individuals are maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This age is derived from hatchery families exhibiting a maximal shell length of 14 centimeters, and it marks the point at which oysters begin contributing to the next generation. The synchrony of this reproductive timing with the thermal regime of the lagoon environment underscores the tight coupling between water temperature and gametogenic cycles in this species.

Longevity records for Pinctada margaritifera indicate that individuals can persist for remarkably extended periods under suitable conditions. Based on comparative data from the closely related Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas, the ultimate age reaches 20 years [am = 20 years] when reared at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This maximum lifespan is considerable for a bivalve and allows for multiple reproductive seasons, enhancing the species' potential for population replenishment. Throughout this lengthy existence, the oysters continue somatic growth, albeit at a decelerating rate, and maintain the capacity for repeated spawning events. The combination of early maturation at one year and a two-decade lifespan (20 years) [am = 20 years] confers a life-history strategy that balances rapid initial reproduction with sustained future fecundity, a pattern well-suited to the variable conditions of tropical reef ecosystems where the species is farmed at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].
